title: Post-quantum signatures, priced
description: This site's TLS key agreement is already post-quantum and its signatures are not. Measuring what ML-DSA-44 and the hash-based alternatives actually cost on the one signature a personal site controls: its own crawler's RFC 9421 request signing.
bodyHtml:
Post-quantum signatures, priced

Half of this site's TLS handshake is already post-quantum and I did nothing to make that happen. The other half, authentication, moves on a completely different schedule, because signatures live in certificates and registries that a personal site does not control. So I went looking for the signature I do control, and measured what it would cost to migrate it.

What is already done, and what it covers

Ask the live site what it negotiated:

$ openssl s_client -connect aadhar.sh:443 -groups X25519MLKEM768 -tls1_3

Negotiated TLS1.3 group: X25519MLKEM768
Peer signature type:     ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256
Certificate:             ecdsa-with-SHA256, P-256

The key agreement is post-quantum. The certificate and the handshake signature are classical, and they will stay that way for a while: no public CA issues ML-DSA certificates into the WebPKI, and Cloudflare's own position is that ML-DSA chains add roughly 14KB per handshake, which is why they are pushing Merkle Tree Certificates instead.

That split matters more than it looks. Key agreement is where harvest now, decrypt later bites: an attacker recording today's ciphertext can decrypt it whenever a quantum computer arrives, so the migration had to happen years early. A signature has no such property. Forging a 2026 signature in 2035 proves nothing about 2026, because by then the request is long over and nobody is still trusting it. The urgency argument for key agreement simply does not transfer.

Three tiers of signature, and only one is mine

SurfaceAlgorithmWhose problem
TLS to visitorsECDSA P-256The CA and browser ecosystem
DNSSEC on the zoneECDSA P-256 SHA-256The registry, plus DNS response sizes
Booking links, cover URLsHMAC-SHA256Already fine. Symmetric, so Grover halves it to 128-bit
AadharshBot request signingEd25519Mine. About 30 lines in one file

AadharshBot signs every outbound request per RFC 9421 using the Web Bot Auth profile, so receiving sites can check that a request really came from here. That signature is the only asymmetric one this site owns end to end. The whole post-quantum question collapses to it.

What the candidates actually cost

Cloudflare's runtime has no post-quantum algorithm in WebCrypto. I checked the shipping binary rather than the docs: workerd 1.20260722 contains the strings Ed25519, X25519, and ECDSA, and no ML-DSA at any parameter size. So this is pure JavaScript, via @noble/post-quantum, signing the site's real signature base on an M3 Max under Node 26.

Cost of one signature

    Flip the toggle before you read on and predict where each bar lands. The point of the exercise is that the ordering changes. SLH-DSA-128s has the smallest public key of anything here at 32 bytes, and it takes two and a half seconds to produce one signature. Its sibling 128f signs in 132ms and spends 22KB of header doing it. There is no row that is small on both axes, which is the actual state of post-quantum signatures rather than a quirk of this library.

    How much of that 8.58ms is the algorithm?

    Less than it looks, and the panel above will prove it on your own hardware if it can. Chrome ships ML-DSA in WebCrypto behind chrome://flags/#webcrypto-pqc, implementing the same WICG proposal whose JWK shape this site already publishes. If that flag is on, the panel offers a button that generates an ML-DSA-44 key in your browser, signs this page's signature base 200 times natively, and drops the result in as a fifth bar next to the JavaScript number.

    This matters for how you read the whole table. The 8.58ms is a ceiling set by running a lattice scheme in a JIT, and the byte counts underneath it are properties of FIPS 204 that no implementation will improve. Sizes are the permanent cost. Speed is the temporary one, and it goes away on its own when the runtimes catch up.

    Why the hash-based options lost

    I wanted SLH-DSA to work. It rests on hash functions alone, so it survives even if lattices turn out to be broken, and its 32-byte public key is charming. It fails here twice over.

    The header is the harder failure. A 128f signature is 22,784 bytes once base64'd into a structured-fields value, and most servers cap total request headers around 8KB, so the crawl would start collecting 431s instead of pages. The latency is the other one: 2.5 seconds of single-threaded work per signature is not something to put in front of an HTTP request, and a Worker bills CPU time.

    Stateful hash-based signatures (LMS, XMSS) fix the size problem and introduce a worse one. Reusing a one-time index is total key compromise, and a Worker isolate is close to the worst place to keep a monotonic counter. I would need a Durable Object doing nothing but handing out indices, and a single replay would end the key. ML-DSA-44 is the only candidate that survives contact with the constraints.

    Shipping it without a codepoint

    Here is the part that made this cheap. The IANA HTTP Signature Algorithms registry has exactly six entries, and every one of them is classical. Cloudflare's Web Bot Auth verifier accepts Ed25519 only and ignores other key types in your directory. An ML-DSA-only signature would be a header nobody on the internet checks.

    But Signature-Input and Signature are structured-fields Dictionaries. A second label appends rather than replaces, so both signatures ride the same request over the same covered components:

    Signature-Input: sig1=("@authority" "signature-agent");created=1785186311;
                   keyid="rn-2026-06-30";alg="ed25519";tag="web-bot-auth",
                 sig2=("@authority" "signature-agent");created=1785186311;
                   keyid="rn-mldsa-2026-07-27";alg="ml-dsa-44";tag="web-bot-auth"

    A verifier that only knows Ed25519 reads sig1 and skips the label it does not recognise. Nothing breaks, and the cost of ignoring sig2 is zero. That property is what makes it defensible to ship an algorithm the registry has not blessed. The token ml-dsa-44 is this site's spelling, chosen to match the registry's existing convention so it slots in if a real registration lands, and /bot says plainly that you should verify sig1 and ignore sig2.

    The public key is published under the same JWKS as an AKP key per RFC 9964, which standardised ML-DSA for JOSE and COSE in May 2026. So the key format is a real standard even though the wire token is not:

    Live, from this site's key directory
    reading /.well-known/http-message-signatures-directory…

    What it costs in production

    About 8.6ms of CPU and 3,228 bytes of request header per signed fetch, plus 11.96KB gzip of lattice code in the Worker bundle, which is the price of carrying an implementation the runtime should be providing. Zero bytes reach a browser, because this is a server-to-server signature and no page loads it. The /around crawl signs roughly 21 origins per refresh, so a full cycle gains around 180ms of CPU on a cached background path.

    Two of those three costs are temporary. When workerd gains native ML-DSA, the bundle cost goes to zero and the signing cost drops to whatever the native bar in the panel above showed you. The 3,228 bytes of header stay forever. That asymmetry is the argument for migrating on the size budget now and letting the speed sort itself out.

    One implementation detail worth stealing: ML-DSA-44 keygen expands a 32-byte seed into a 2,560-byte secret key and costs about 1.4ms. Worker isolates outlive a request, so the expanded key is derived once and cached in module scope, keyed by the raw secret so a rotation inside a live isolate re-derives instead of signing with a retired key.

    The objection I think is right

    The strongest reading of this page is that it is theatre. Nothing verifies sig2. Signatures have no harvest-now-decrypt-later exposure, so there is no clock forcing the migration. By that argument the honest move was to write the analysis and ship nothing.

    I mostly agree, and it is why sig2 is second rather than first, why a missing key degrades to Ed25519 alone instead of failing the request, and why /bot tells verifiers to ignore it. What I get in exchange is a migration already paid for and measured, on a surface where being wrong costs a crawl rather than a login. When the registry does land a codepoint, the remaining work is renaming a string.

    What would change my mind: a receiving server rejecting requests because the extra 3.2KB pushes headers past its limit, or a verifier that chokes on a dictionary label it does not know. Either result would mean a second label is not free after all, and sig2 would come straight back out. The crawl logs are where that would show up first.

    What actually happened: retired after 19 days

    Neither of those things went wrong. No server rejected the headers, and no verifier choked on the extra label. The prediction above was accurate and it was aimed in the wrong direction, because it priced the cost to other people and treated the cost to this site as a settled line item: 8.58ms, listed once, in a table.

    The number that mattered was 8.58ms multiplied by fan-out, against a per-invocation budget. This site runs on the Workers free plan, which allows 10ms of CPU per request. So one signature spent most of a request's entire budget, and every surface that signs more than once had already blown it:

    SurfaceSignatures per requestML-DSA CPU
    A single crawl of one origin1~8.5ms of a 10ms budget
    The /rn playlist scrape21, one per track~180ms
    /lens discovery28 probes~240ms

    Both of those were dark and neither said so. The playlist scrape catches a failed track embed per track and degrades that one track to no cover, so 21 signatures timing out rendered as a tracklist that had quietly stopped showing album art. On /lens it was louder but no better attributed: sampling production logs on 2026-08-15, 31 of 51 requests died exceededCpu, nearly all of them /lens/fetch and /lens/tools.

    Removing sig2 took the scrape from 379ms of CPU to 95ms, measured on the same 21-track playlist. The key is out of the JWKS too, because publishing a key nothing signs with is the dangling-pointer problem this site refuses elsewhere.

    The honest reading is that the objection above was right for a reason it did not name. Shipping the migration early was cheap to build and the build was never the risk. What it cost was a recurring tax on every outbound request, on the one axis a free-tier Worker has least of, and the page that measured the tax in isolation is the same page that missed it in aggregate. A per-request cost is only a number once you know how many requests, and how much budget.

    None of this changes the sizing argument, which is the part worth keeping. The 3,228 bytes are still permanent, the speed is still temporary, and when workerd ships native ML-DSA the CPU objection evaporates and sig2 can come back with no code to write beyond deleting this section. Until then the migration is measured, documented, and turned off.

editorial.reader: Someone who has read that post-quantum migration is coming and wants to know what it costs on a real surface rather than in a roadmap.
editorial.problem: The reader can name ML-DSA and SLH-DSA without knowing which one survives an HTTP request, or which parts of their own stack they could even change.
editorial.thesis: Post-quantum signing is affordable exactly where you control both ends, and RFC 9421's dictionary fields let a second signature ship years before the registry blesses it.
evidence: The live TLS handshake shows post-quantum key agreement alongside a classical P-256 certificate, which locates the gap precisely.
Signature size and signing time are measured for ML-DSA-44, both SLH-DSA parameter sets, and Ed25519 on the site's real signature base.
SLH-DSA-128f needs 22,784 bytes of header and SLH-DSA-128s needs 2.5 seconds per signature, so each fails a different hard constraint.
Readers whose browser has Chrome's post-quantum WebCrypto flag on can run the native implementation in place and see how much of the JavaScript timing was the runtime rather than the algorithm.
The page reads the site's own key directory at load time, so the published ML-DSA key it reports is the key the crawler signs with.
editorial.uncertainty: Retired on 2026-08-15 after 19 days. Nothing on the internet ever rejected the larger headers, which is what this page watched for. What ended it was CPU: ~8.5ms of pure-JS signing per request against a 10ms per-invocation budget, multiplied by fan-out, which had silently taken down the playlist scrape and the /lens discovery pass. The sizing argument is unaffected and the label can return when workerd ships native ML-DSA.

understanding.intro: Before you close the hood: four questions about why this shipped and what it does not buy.

questions.q: Why can this site send an ML-DSA signature years before IANA registers a post-quantum algorithm?

options.t: Signature-Input and Signature are structured-fields Dictionaries, so a second label appends and an old verifier reads the label it knows.
options.why: Right. Additive labels are what make an unregistered algorithm safe to send: ignoring it costs a verifier nothing.

options.t: RFC 9421 lets a sender pick any algorithm as long as the key is published in a JWKS.
options.why: Publishing a key does not make an algorithm interoperable. The registry is what tells a verifier which token means which algorithm.

options.t: Cloudflare verifies ML-DSA signatures already, so the registry no longer matters.
options.why: Cloudflare's Web Bot Auth verifier accepts Ed25519 only and ignores other key types in the directory.

questions.q: Both SLH-DSA parameter sets were rejected. What does comparing them tell you about hash-based signatures here?

options.t: They trade signing time against signature size, so one blows the header limit and the other blows the latency budget.
options.why: Right. 128f signs in 132ms but needs 22,784 bytes of header; 128s is compact by comparison and takes 2.5 seconds. Neither is small on both axes.

options.t: Hash-based signatures have large public keys, which is what makes them impractical for HTTP.
options.why: Their public keys are the smallest on the page at 32 bytes. The signatures are what fail.

options.t: Both are slower to verify than ML-DSA, so receiving sites would reject them.
options.why: Verification is in the same few-millisecond range for all of them. The binding constraints are signing time and signature size.

questions.q: This site's TLS already negotiates X25519MLKEM768. What does that protect, and what does it leave open?

options.t: It protects confidentiality against an attacker recording traffic today, and leaves authentication on a classical P-256 certificate.
options.why: Right. Key agreement had to migrate early because recorded ciphertext can be decrypted later. The certificate chain is a separate, slower migration.

options.t: It makes the whole handshake post-quantum, including the certificate.
options.why: The handshake still reports ecdsa_secp256r1_sha256 and a P-256 certificate. Only the key agreement moved.

options.t: It protects the crawler's outbound request signatures.
options.why: Those are application-layer RFC 9421 signatures. TLS key agreement has no bearing on them.

questions.q: Why is there less urgency to migrate a request signature than to migrate key agreement?

options.t: A recorded request cannot be retroactively forged into something anyone still trusts, while recorded ciphertext can be decrypted whenever the hardware arrives.
options.why: Right. Harvest now, decrypt later applies to confidentiality. An ephemeral signature stops mattering once the request is served.

options.t: Request signatures use stronger keys than TLS key agreement does.
options.why: Ed25519 and X25519 sit at comparable classical strength. The difference is what an attacker gains by breaking each one later.

options.t: Signatures are verified locally, so a quantum attacker could never reach them.
options.why: A forger with the private key could sign anything. The reason the clock is slower is that a stale forgery buys nothing.

questions.q: The page reports 8.58ms to sign and 2,420 bytes of signature. Which of those two numbers should you expect to improve, and why?

options.t: The time, because it measures a lattice scheme running in JavaScript, while the size is fixed by FIPS 204.
options.why: Right. A native implementation changes the timing and cannot change the byte count, which is why the migration decision should rest on the size budget.

options.t: The size, because compression will shrink the signature once it travels as a header.
options.why: Signature bytes are effectively random, so they do not compress. The base64 expansion makes the header larger rather than smaller.

options.t: Neither, because both are properties of ML-DSA-44 as standardised.
options.why: Only the sizes are standardised. The 8.58ms belongs to this implementation on this hardware, which is what the in-browser native run demonstrates.

questions.q: Which result would falsify this page's claim that the second signature is free to ignore?

options.t: A receiving server rejecting the crawl because the extra 3.2KB pushes the request past its header limit.
options.why: Right, and that is the check the page committed to. It never fired: no server rejected the headers. sig2 came out anyway on 2026-08-15, for a cost this page measured once and never multiplied, which is ~8.5ms of signing CPU per request against a 10ms per-invocation budget. Read the retirement section.

options.t: A verifier reading sig1 and ignoring sig2 entirely.
options.why: That is the predicted behaviour, so it supports the model rather than challenging it.

options.t: IANA registering a different token for ML-DSA in the signature algorithms registry.
options.why: That would mean renaming a string. The page already treats its own token as provisional.
